title: Discovering Iceland: A Week in the Land of Fire and Ice
excerpt: Iceland has always held a special allure for me—a land where fire and ice coexist in stunning harmony. During my week-long adventure, I found myself captivated by its otherworldly landscapes: bubbling geysers, majestic glaciers, and dramatic volcanic craters that seemed to tell stories of ancient forces at play. Each day unfolded new wonders, from hiking along breathtaking cliffs to soaking in natural hot springs. Join me on this journey as I share the unforgettable experiences and moments that made my time in Iceland truly magical.

seoTitle: Iceland Itinerary 1 Week: Blue Lagoon to Glaciers
seoDescription: My Iceland itinerary 1 week: Blue Lagoon, south coast waterfalls, Jökulsárlón, a glacier hike and the Golden Circle, plus driving and safety tips.
contentHtml:
Iceland is a country of stunning natural beauty, rich culture, and friendly people. It has been on my bucket list for a long time, and I finally got the chance to visit it with my friends David and Gabby. We spent a week exploring some of the most amazing sights and experiences that Iceland has to offer, and I want to share them with you in this blog post.

Iceland trip at a glance

  • Trip length: About a week, with my friends David and Gabby
  • Base: A hotel in Laugardalur, Reykjavík
  • Getting around: Buses and guided tours, then a rental car on Day 5
  • Highlights: Blue Lagoon, Seljalandsfoss and Skógafoss, Reynisfjara black sand beach, Jökulsárlón glacier lagoon, a Sólheimajökull glacier hike, Þingvellir National Park, Geysir and Strokkur, and the Fagradalsfjall volcano
  • Airport: Keflavík International Airport (KEF), about 50 km (31 miles) from Reykjavík
  • Currency: Icelandic króna (ISK)
  • Emergency number: 112

Day 1: Arrival and Blue Lagoon

Arrival and Laugardalur Park

We arrived at Reykjavik airport in the morning, and took a bus to our hotel located in Laugardalur, a green and peaceful area of the city. After checking in and resting for a bit, we had a hearty breakfast at the hotel, and then relaxed for a while. We also visited the Laugardalur Park, where we rode scooters and explored the botanical garden, the zoo, and the sculpture garden.

View from bus going to Reykjavík

Blue Lagoon

In the afternoon, we took a bus to the Blue Lagoon, one of the most famous attractions in Iceland. Blue Lagoon is a geothermal spa located in Iceland, specifically in a lava field in Grindavík, on the Reykjanes Peninsula in southwestern Iceland. The mineral-rich seawater creates a milky blue color and a soothing effect on the skin.

We spent a couple of hours soaking in the lagoon, applying the silica mud mask, and enjoying the views of the volcanic landscape. It was a truly relaxing and rejuvenating experience.

Dinner at Kopar by the Old Harbor

After the lagoon, we took a bus back to Reykjavik, and had dinner at Kopar, a grill and cocktail bar by the old harbor. I had the carrot soup and the cod fish, which were both delicious and fresh. David and Gabby had the adventure menu, which consisted of nine courses of creative and delicious dishes, such as rock crab soup, lamb fillet, and chocolate cake.

We also enjoyed the live music and the cozy atmosphere. It was a perfect way to end the day. After dinner, we walked around the harbor and noticed that it was still bright outside, even though it was 11:30 pm.

We learned that Iceland has a phenomenon called the midnight sun, where the sun never sets completely during the summer months. This means that there are long hours of daylight, and sometimes the sky changes colors from pink to orange to blue. It was a magical sight that we will never forget.

Day 2: Waterfalls, Black Beach, and Glacier Lagoon

On our second day in Iceland, we explored some of the most stunning natural attractions on the south coast. We saw two majestic waterfalls, a dramatic black sand beach, and a mesmerizing glacier lagoon. It was a day full of awe and adventure!

Iceland is a country of waterfalls, with over 10,000 of them scattered across the land. Some are larger than others, and some plummet into small blue pools while others dribble over moss-covered rocks or lava fields.

We explored two of the most spectacular waterfalls in the country: Seljalandsfoss and Skogafoss. We were amazed by their beauty and power, and we had fun viewing them from various points and levels. The highlight of our day was walking behind Seljalandsfoss, which gave us a unique and stunning perspective.

Seljalandsfoss Waterfalls

We also learned that Seljalandsfoss is one of the many waterfalls in Iceland that are fed by the melting glaciers.

Skogafoss Waterfalls

Our next stop was Skogafoss, another impressive waterfall that is 60 meters tall and 25 meters wide. We climbed up the stairs to the top of the waterfall, where we had a panoramic view of the surrounding landscape.

Reynisfjara Black Sand Beach

After the waterfalls, we continued to the black sand beach of Reynisfjara, where we saw the striking contrast between the dark sand and the white waves. We also admired the basalt columns and the rock formations of Reynisdrangar, which are said to be the remains of trolls that were turned to stone by the sunlight. We were careful not to get too close to the water, as the waves can be very powerful and dangerous.

Jökulsárlón Glacier Lagoon

Our final destination of the day was Höfn í Hornafirði, a town near the glacier lagoon of Jokulsarlon. The glacier lagoon is a stunning sight, where huge blocks of ice break off from the glacier and float in the water. We took a boat ride on the lagoon, and got to see the icebergs up close, and even got to hold a piece of ice for some pictures. It was amazing to see the different shapes, colors, and sizes of the ice, and to learn about the history and ecology of the glacier.

It was a long day of driving and sightseeing, but we were rewarded with some of the most breathtaking views and experiences of our lives. We returned to our hotel in Laugardalur, tired but happy, and rested for the next day.

Day 4: Sunrise, Glacier Hike, and Downtown

Sunrise at Hallgrímskirkja

The fourth day was another early start, as we wanted to catch the sunrise at Hallgrimskirkja, the iconic church that dominates the skyline of Reykjavik. We walked to the church from our hotel, and climbed up the tower, where we had a spectacular view of the city and the mountains. The sunrise was one of the best we had ever seen, with the sky changing colors from pink to orange to blue. It was a magical moment that we will never forget.

Sólheimajökull Glacier Hike

After the sunrise, we joined another guided tour that took us to the Solheimajokull glacier, where we did a three-hour glacier hike. We put on our crampons, helmets, and harnesses, and followed our guide on the ice.

We learned how to walk on the glacier, how to use the ice axe, and how to avoid the crevasses. We also saw some amazing features of the glacier, such as ice caves, moulins, and moraines. It was a thrilling and educational adventure that made us appreciate the beauty and power of nature.

Downtown Reykjavík and Dinner at Matarkjallarinn

At night, we explored the downtown area of Reykjavik, where we saw the colorful houses, the street art, and the quirky shops.

We also had dinner at Matarkjallarinn, a cozy and elegant restaurant that serves Icelandic and international cuisine. We had the tasting menu, which included dishes such as smoked puffin, grilled lamb, and skyr cheesecake.

We also enjoyed the live jazz music and the friendly service. It was a great way to end the day.

Day 5: National Park, Geysers, and Volcano

Þingvellir National Park

The fifth day was our last full day in Iceland, and we wanted to make the most of it. We rented a car and drove to the Thingvellir National Park, where we saw the rift valley between the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates. We walked along the Althing, the site of the oldest parliament in the world, and saw the Oxararfoss waterfall, the Thingvallavatn lake, and the Silfra fissure. We also learned about the historical and cultural significance of the park, which is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Geysir and Strokkur

After the park, we drove to the Haukadalur geothermal area, where we saw the famous geysers of Geysir and Strokkur. Geysir is the original geyser that gave its name to all the others, but it is mostly dormant now. Strokkur, on the other hand, erupts every few minutes, shooting a jet of hot water and steam into the air. We watched the geysers for a while, and also saw the bubbling mud pools, the steaming vents, and the colorful minerals.

Fagradalsfjall Volcano

Our final stop of the day was Grindavik, where we saw the Fagradalsfjall volcano, which had been erupting since March 2021. We hiked to a safe viewing point, where we saw the lava flowing from the crater and forming new land. We also felt the heat and heard the sound of the eruption. It was an awe-inspiring and humbling sight, and we felt lucky to witness it.

We drove back to our hotel, packed our bags, and prepared for our departure the next day.

Day 6: Departure and Farewell

The sixth day was our departure day, and we had to say goodbye to Iceland. We checked out of our hotel, took a bus to the airport, and boarded our flight back home. We were sad to leave, but we were also grateful for the amazing week we had in Iceland. We made some unforgettable memories, saw some incredible sights, and had some fun adventures. We also learned a lot about the country, its people, and its culture. We agreed that Iceland was one of the best places we had ever visited, and that we would love to come back someday.

Know before you go: Iceland travel tips

Best time to visit

It depends on what you want to see. Summer days are extremely long. Around the June solstice, Reykjavík gets about 21 hours of daylight, which is why it was still bright when we walked the harbor at 11:30 PM. Summer is also when the highland F-roads open, usually in late June or early July.

Around the December solstice, Reykjavík gets only about 4 hours of daylight. The trade-off is the northern lights. Visit Iceland puts aurora season from late August to late April, and you need darkness plus clear or partly clear skies. The aurora shows up most often around 11 PM, so plan to be outside from roughly 10 PM to 1 AM.

Winter conditions are not limited to winter. Snow and ice can also show up in spring and autumn, so build some flexibility into any road trip.

Getting there and getting around

  • Airport transfer: Keflavík International Airport (KEF) is about 50 km from Reykjavík. The Flybus is timed to every arriving flight and takes around 45 minutes to the BSÍ bus terminal in Reykjavík, with optional hotel drop-off.
  • Tours vs. driving: Guided tours are an easy way to see the south coast and the glaciers without driving yourself. If you rent a car, be well rested first. Safetravel points out that many visitors feel jet lagged after an overnight flight from America. My guide to overcoming jet lag can help.
  • Speed limits: 50 km/h in towns, 80 km/h on rural gravel roads, and 90 km/h on paved rural roads unless signs say otherwise. Headlights must be on at all times, all year, and the blood alcohol limit (0.02%) means you can’t drive even after one drink.
  • Single-lane bridges: They are common on and off the Ring Road. The speed limit across them is 50 km/h, and the car closer to the bridge has the right of way.
  • Road conditions: Check umferdin.is (road.is) before every drive, or call the 24-hour road information line at 1777. Google Maps and other map apps don’t always show closed or impassable roads.

F-roads and highland driving

  • F-roads are Iceland’s mountain roads. They are usually closed from mid-September until June or July, and they only open once the ground has properly thawed. Driving on a closed road can bring heavy fines.
  • You need a suitable 4x4, and not every 4x4 works for every F-road. Some routes are only passable in a modified super jeep.
  • Many F-roads have unbridged rivers. No insurance covers damage to a vehicle while crossing a river, so if you are unsure, turn around.
  • Off-road driving is strictly forbidden. F-roads and gravel roads are fine; driving off them is not.

Weather and safety

  • Forecasts and alerts: Check the Icelandic Met Office at vedur.is for the weather and Safetravel for current alerts. Conditions can change fast.
  • Emergencies: Call 112. If a 112 call won’t connect, Safetravel lists 599-0112 as a backup number. The 112 Iceland app is designed to speed up getting information to responders in an emergency.
  • Reynisfjara: Sneaker waves can surge far up the beach with zero warning. Warning lights at the entrance show the current level: yellow means stay alert, orange means stay at least 25 m (82 ft) from the sea, and red means the beach is closed beyond the viewing area. Never turn your back on the sea, and watch for falling rock near the cliffs.
  • Glaciers: Safetravel recommends going with a guide who knows the area well. It currently warns that conditions at the edge of Sólheimajökull are changing rapidly, with an unstable ice ridge and a risk of rockfall, so check before you book.
  • Blue Lagoon and Reykjanes: Pre-booking the Blue Lagoon is essential. It sits in a seismically active area and has built protective barriers against potential lava flows, so check the latest updates before you go.
  • Þingvellir: A parking service fee applies at the lots closest to the most popular sights.

What to pack

  • Layers: a warm base layer, a fleece or light insulated jacket, and a waterproof, windproof shell
  • Waterproof shoes with good grip for waterfall spray (especially if you walk behind Seljalandsfoss like we did) and black sand beaches
  • A swimsuit for the Blue Lagoon
  • A hat and gloves for glacier hikes and northern lights nights
  • A sleep mask if you visit around midsummer, when it barely gets dark

Want to pack lighter for a trip like this? Here is how I travel comfortably with minimal luggage. And if Iceland is calling you, it is also on my lists of top adventure travel destinations and best solo travel destinations for first-time travelers.

Final thoughts

I hope you enjoyed reading about our trip to Iceland, and that it inspired you to visit this wonderful country yourself. If you have any questions or comments, please feel free to leave them below. Thank you for reading!
